claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its ternary and quaternary subsets are governed by local chemical fluctuations.
Local chemical fluctuations change chemical short-range order.
Changes in short-range order cause corresponding changes in stacking-fault energy.
Stacking-fault energy affects dislocation slip, mechanical twinning, and strain-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Intermediate stacking-fault energy promotes mechanical twinning, whereas sufficiently low stacking-fault energy promotes FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Intrinsic chemical variation can promote three-dimensional stacking-fault networks involved in an FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Reducing constituent count alters the local chemical environment and defect energetics.
Ternary and quaternary subsets may exhibit more short-range order than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Enhanced short-range order in lower-constituent alloys may produce locally lower stacking-fault energy.
The equiatomic quinary baseline has more statistically random site occupancy than its ternary and quaternary subsets.
CrCoNi differs from CrCoMnFeNi in relative FCC-versus-HCP stability, with HCP identified as the CrCoNi ground state and magnetic frustration affecting the quinary alloy.
Selected ternary or quaternary alloys will exhibit different onset, density, and evolution of twins and stacking-fault networks relative to the quinary baseline.
Selected subsets may form HCP regions earlier or more extensively than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Greater activation of twinning or transformation-induced plasticity would enhance strain hardening and could alter ductility.
Chemical, magnetic, and crystallographic factors may jointly affect the deformation behavior.
Restricting samples to single-phase FCC microstructures with minimal secondary phases isolates the proposed compositional-fluctuation effects.
APT can quantitatively map both local chemical fluctuations and short-range order in the proposed samples.
Local stacking-fault-energy distributions can be determined from diffraction peak shifts and defect densities.

Absence of statistically significant differences in short-range order, stacking-fault-energy distributions, and defect nucleation between the baseline and subsets would falsify the proposed mechanism.
